Name for the term: "thức ăn sống"
Name for the term: "Live Foods"
Live food moves, which encourages fish to eat; it gives fish physical and mental enrichment and is a fast way to condition them for breeding.
Merck says live feeds can be varied with diverse commercially prepared feeds, so fish do not eat only one kind of food.
Feeding only one type of food can cause nutrient deficiencies; a varied diet is recommended.
Feeding only one kind of food leads to nutrient shortfalls, slow growth and poor colour; foods should be rotated.
Relying only on live food for fry is a mistake; dry food should be introduced later so fish learn a varied diet.
Overfeeding live food fouls the water; uneaten food should be removed and waste siphoned regularly because it decays.
Feed fry so they finish the food within 5-10 minutes; overfeeding causes constipation, gut inflammation and water pollution.
Live food that is not washed well can carry parasites.
Store-bought feeder fish are more likely to spread disease to an aquarium, and most keepers do not quarantine them.
Goldfish and minnows sold as feeders contain high thiaminase, which can block thiamin (vitamin B1) and cause health problems.
Merck says commercial frozen feeds such as brine shrimp, bloodworms, mysids or glassworms should be discarded after 1 year, and thawed feeds should not be refrozen.
trùn chỉ: the Vietnamese name a CTU Journal study uses for the oligochaete worm Limnodrilus hoffmeisteri.
trùn chỉ (Limnodrilus hoffmeisteri) feeds on detritus and lives at high density on the bottoms of freshwater bodies; in aquaculture it is fed to fish and crustaceans at first feeding.
trùn chỉ (Limnodrilus hoffmeisteri) grown in the laboratory for 42 days did best on rice bran (biomass up about 4.53 times, density about 9.12 times), and worst on chicken and cow manure.
trùn chỉ sold as ornamental fish food is collected by hand from the mud of the Chà Và River in Sóc Trăng, a river described as black, foul-smelling and polluted with waste and toilet discharge.
trùn chỉ collectors in Sóc Trăng sell at 25,000-30,000 VND/kg, and aquarium shops sell the worms at 500-1,000 VND per bag.
trùn chỉ collectors on the Chà Và River put the worms in a covered container for about 120 minutes so they rise, then scoop them into cleaner water.
trùn chỉ were harvested by diving and scooping mud in rivers around Ho Chi Minh City (quận 8, Bình Chánh, Bình Triệu, Thanh Đa) in a 2004 report.
trùn chỉ live only in water that carries silt and is clean and free of acid sulfate (phèn) contamination, according to a 2004 report from Ho Chi Minh City.
Trùn chỉ: rinse with clean water, then dip in dilute salt water for about 2-3 minutes to remove parasites and bacteria (no salt concentration given).
Trùn chỉ easily carry bacteria and parasites if not washed thoroughly.
Tubifex worms harvested from sewers, open water or hatcheries may be infected with various diseases and can be vectors for whirling disease of salmonids (statement tagged citation needed).
Tubifex: keeping the worms under brisk running water until they void their gut contents can partly reduce the disease risk.
Tubifex are very fattening and poor in some essential amino acids; fish fed mostly on them may be less healthy and colourful.
Tubifex live in lake and river sediments and occasionally in sewer lines; Tubifex tubifex is raised commercially mainly as fish food.
Tubifex can become a pest in poorly cleaned aquaria, forming a thick carpet on the bottom.
BoBo is also called "bọ nước" and refers to the genera Moina and Daphnia.
BoBo: filter through fine mesh and rinse several times with clean water, then feed in several small portions a day.
Natural BoBo may carry bacteria and pollute water; the page suggests dipping in dilute salt water or light gentian violet but gives no concentration or time.
Feeding dead or foul-smelling BoBo can cause disease in fry.
BoBo can be fed to fry 3-5 days old, which can take larger food than Artemia; protein up to 60%.
Daphnia are aquatic crustaceans about 1–5 mm long, suited to small and medium fish.

Daphnia culture: use old tank water or aged dechlorinated water because they are very chlorine-sensitive; about 68°F (20°C) and long light exposure; feed active dry yeast, green water or spirulina once the water is no longer cloudy; harvest with a fine net.
Artemia is also called "tôm ngâm nước muối"; "cyst" is the egg and "nauplii" the newly hatched larvae.
Artemia (Artemia spp.) is also called "khỉ biển", a small crustacean; species named are "A.Salina" and "A.Franciscana".
Bo bo (Artemia): one Vietnamese article uses this name for Artemia salina, also calling it "cua nước muối", while another uses BoBo for Moina and Daphnia.
Artemia: hatch cysts 24 hours in 25–28°C salt water with strong aeration (24–36 hours overall); sieve through fine mesh and rinse with clean water before feeding.
Artemia: hatch with about 25–30 g salt per litre, 25–28°C, pH 7.5–8.5, continuous aeration, for 18–36 hours; separate larvae from shells with light or a filter and rinse with clean water.
Baby brine shrimp (Artemia): soak eggs in salt water at 74–82°F (23–28°C) for about 18–36 hours; shine a light at the base of the hatchery to separate shrimp from shells.
Ấu trùng Artemia: use 30g non-iodized salt per 1L of fresh water if no seawater, about 1g eggs per 1L; light the hatcher for the first 24 hours; nauplii appear after about 16–20 hours.
Ấu trùng Artemia harvest: turn off the air and let it settle; shells float and nauplii sink; shine a flashlight on the bottom and siphon the nauplii.
Ấu trùng Artemia: keep strong aeration only at first; once eggs hydrate, reduce it so eggs are not blown out.
Ấu trùng Artemia: the yolk is used up after about 24 hours.
Bo bo (Artemia): hatch with 25-30 g salt per litre, 1-2 teaspoons of eggs, aeration, 26-28°C and strong light; eggs hatch after 24-48 hours.
Artemia: leftover nauplii should be frozen right after hatching and stored sealed, away from light and moisture.
Artemia: using old Artemia can harm fish health, digestion and growth; overfeeding pollutes the water.
Artemia: poor-quality eggs or nauplii show pale colour, an odd smell, slow hatching, and weak larvae that swim slowly or die in large numbers.
Artemia: healthy nauplii swim toward light and have full guts (keeper report).
Artemia: uneaten nauplii decay and produce ammonia and nitrite; do not overfeed (keeper report).
Artemia Vĩnh Châu, from Vĩnh Châu, Sóc Trăng, is named by Vietnamese keepers as a local Artemia source.
Artemia: nauplii are about 0.4 mm, suited to fry 1–2 days old; protein 55–65%.

Blackworms: on arrival rinse in a fine net with dechlorinated water chilled to 40–55°F (4–13°C); keep in a shallow container no more than 0.5 inches (1.3 cm) deep under cold dechlorinated water in the fridge, and rinse daily with prechilled water.
Blackworms not rinsed daily will quickly foul the water.
Blackworms sink to the bottom and many breeders consider them the best way to condition Corydoras.

Vinegar eels: culture in a long-necked bottle of 50% apple cider vinegar, 50% dechlorinated water and apple slices; harvest by putting filter floss and dechlorinated water in the neck and pipetting the eels that swim up.
Micro worms: culture in small plastic containers on instant mashed potatoes, with a breathing hole in the lid plugged with filter floss.

Infusoria: fill a jar with old tank water plus filter mulm, add a 1-inch piece of banana peel or ½ teaspoon instant yeast, warm to 78–80°F (26–27°C); harvest with a pipette when the water turns from cloudy to clear.
Grindal and white worms: skipping sterilisation of the substrate (180–200°F, 82–93°C) lets mites and other pests in.
Mosquito larvae: set out a 5-gallon bucket of dechlorinated water for mosquitoes to lay eggs and scoop larvae daily with a fine net; not harvesting daily lets them become adult mosquitoes.
Snails as live food need hard water with higher pH and GH; in soft water add crushed coral or minerals or their shells may develop holes.
